activities.caption: pair each dial with what it sets
activities.name: quadDialMatch

config.prompt: The parabola y = a·x² + b·x + c has three dials — pair each with its role:

pairs.right: how fast the bowl opens — its sign decides up or down
tilts the axis of symmetry off centre
where the curve starts on the y-axis

config.why: Slide a to exactly 0 and the parabola degenerates into a straight line — a quadratic is a linear function with one extra term, and the extra term is where all the new behaviour lives.

activities.caption: file each claim under its tool
activities.name: quadToolSort

config.prompt: File each claim under the solving tool it describes:

items.label: fastest when it works — the roots leap out in one line
always works, and yields the vertex form as a free gift
completing the square done once, for every quadratic at once
the right tool when the question also asks for the vertex

config.why: Each tool has its moment: try factorising first, check the discriminant before computing, and complete the square when the vertex is wanted.

activities.anchor: look for two numbers that multiply to c and add to b
activities.caption: fill the blanks — the factorising search rule
activities.name: quadFactorCloze

config.text: The search rule for x² + 6x − 7: look for two numbers that multiply to %%0%% and add to %%1%% — here +7 and −1 — and the roots leap out as x = 1 or x = −7.
config.hint: The constant term, and the middle coefficient.

config.prompt: One of these claims about square-rooting is wrong — click it:
lines: From (x + 3)² = 16, the answers are x + 3 = +4 and x + 3 = −4.
The squaring step genuinely destroyed information.
Dropping the minus sign loses no roots — the negative root is extraneous.
config.correction: Dropping the minus loses half the roots — the single most common quadratic error.
config.why: Both signs fed the same square, so both must be kept; the ± means two answers unless the discriminant says otherwise.

activities.anchor: there are no real roots and no crossings
activities.caption: the floating parabola
activities.name: quadDiscBranch

config.root: For y = x² + 2x + 5, the discriminant is 4 − 20 = −16. How many real roots?

choices.label: Two — every quadratic has two roots
choices.feedback: No: a negative number has no real square root — the parabola floats entirely above the axis, with no crossings.

choices.label: None — the curve never touches the axis
choices.feedback: Right — and it is information, not error: a bridge deck's load curve that never crosses zero is the discriminant keeping the bridge up.

choices.label: One — the vertex touches zero
choices.feedback: One root needs the discriminant exactly 0 — the repeated root sitting at the vertex.

two.text: Two roots need a positive discriminant — two real crossings.

none.text: Verify the arithmetic, then let the sign tell you the geometry.

one.text: y = x² − 4x + 4 = (x − 2)² is the zero-discriminant case: it kisses the axis at x = 2.

config.why: The discriminant b² − 4ac counts the crossings before you compute — the arithmetic shadow of the geometry.

activities.anchor: the vertex lies midway between them
activities.caption: call the vertex's x
activities.name: quadVertexEst

config.prompt: For y = x² − 4x + 3, the roots are 1 and 3 and the vertex lies midway between them. At what x does the vertex sit?
config.why: x = −b/2a = 2, where y = 4 − 8 + 3 = −1 — four facts, one smooth symmetric bowl.
config.context: it crosses the y-axis at c = 3 and opens up (a = 1)

activities.caption: bet before you read on — the profit vertex
activities.name: quadProfitPredict

config.q: Profit is P = −2x² + 120x − 1,000, with vertex at x = 30. Because a is negative, that vertex is…
choices: a maximum — 800 in profit at 30 units
a minimum — the worst point to sell
config.why: A negative a makes a hill: the bowl opens down, so the vertex is a maximum. Calling x = 30 the 'minimum profit' would invert the entire business decision.

activities.anchor: the gradient at a point is the gradient of the
activities.caption: drop the marker — where the tangent flattens
activities.name: quadTangentPlace

config.prompt: For y = x², at what x is the tangent exactly horizontal?
config.why: The gradient 2a·x + b is zero at the vertex — the flattest point of a parabola is a single instant, not a flat section.

activities.anchor: Throw a ball straight up at 20 m/s
activities.caption: rebuild the thrown-ball analysis
activities.name: quadBallOrder

config.prompt: Rebuild the analysis of h = 20t − 4.9t² — what comes first:
items: Read the roots: t = 0 (the throw) and t ≈ 4.08 s (the landing)
Vertex at t = −b/2a ≈ 2.04 s — exactly half the flight
Velocity at the top is zero — the tangent is horizontal
config.why: Roots are launch and landing, the vertex is the apex, the symmetry axis is mid-flight: quadratics model anything with constant acceleration.

activities.caption: find the shortcut that deletes a root
activities.name: quadDivideSpot

config.prompt: One of these claims about the x² = 3x trap is wrong — click it:
lines: Dividing both sides by x lands on a correct half-answer: x = 3.
The division silently assumes x is not zero.
x = 0 is a genuine solution — the other half of the truth.
Dividing by x is fine here because the equation is quadratic.
config.correction: Never divide by the thing you are solving for — factor out instead: x(x − 3) = 0 gives both answers, 0 and 3.
config.why: Quadratics punish shortcuts; they reward the checklist.
